title: Which two numbers have HCF one and LCM sixty six?
description: Two numbers must have a highest common factor of one and a lowest common multiple of sixty six. Sixty six is broken into primes, and each prime is given to only one of the two numbers. The pair is checked against both conditions.
teaching_notes: One idea: a highest common factor of one means the two numbers share no prime, so every prime of the lowest common multiple goes to exactly one number. Ask the class to break sixty six into primes before the working is shown. Watch for students who give the same prime to both numbers.

source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q4
video_script.why: The child has read a highest common factor and a lowest common multiple from prime counts and now works backwards from them to find two numbers.
video_script.substitution: Break the lowest common multiple into primes and give each prime to only one number, because the highest common factor is one.
video_script.anchor: The numbers one and sixty six in two boxes labelled highest common factor and lowest common multiple, with two empty number boxes beside them.
video_script.payoff_line: Two such numbers are six and eleven

final_answer.value: For example 6 and 11 (also 1 and 66, 2 and 33, 3 and 22)
final_answer.spoken: for example six and eleven, and also one and sixty six, two and thirty three, and three and twenty two

hold_back: For example 6 and 11 (also 1 and 66, 2 and 33, 3 and 22)
never_show: a pair that shares a prime
maths_rules: HCF = 1 means every smaller count is 0, so no prime is in both numbers
LCM takes the larger counts, so each of 2, 3 and 11 is in exactly one number, once
check: 66 ÷ 6 = 11 and 66 ÷ 11 = 6; 6 = 2 × 3 and 11 share no prime, so HCF = 1 and LCM = 2 × 3 × 11 = 66
video_script.design: One idea: a highest common factor of one means no shared prime, so each prime of the lowest common multiple goes to one number only. The prime split stays on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We must find two numbers that fit both of these facts.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The largest number that divides both numbers is called their highest common factor. In this question it is the number one.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The smallest number that is a multiple of both is called their lowest common multiple. In this question it is the number sixty six.

marks.m2: two numbers are shown in prime columns

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Every number can be broken into primes, which are numbers whose only factors are one and itself.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We count how many times each prime appears in each number.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The highest common factor takes the smaller count of each prime. The lowest common multiple takes the larger count.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the highest common factor is one and the lowest common multiple is sixty six.

beats.on_screen: To find: two numbers with this HCF and LCM

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find two such numbers. We solve it the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, break sixty six into primes. It is two times three times eleven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: HCF = 1, so every smaller count is 0 and no prime is in both numbers

marks.m1: the smaller count of every prime is written as 0
marks.m2: the words no prime is in both numbers are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the highest common factor is one. Every smaller count must be zero.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>This means no prime is in both numbers.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: the LCM takes the larger counts, so 2, 3 and 11 each go to one number only. Give 2 and 3 to the first and 11 to the second

marks.m1: the primes 2, 3 and 11 are written, each with count 1
marks.m2: 2 and 3 are placed in the first number box
marks.m3: 11 is placed in the second number box

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the lowest common multiple takes the larger counts. Two, three and eleven each appear once.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each one must go to only one number. Give two and three to the first number.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Give eleven to the second number, and keep it away from the first.

marks.m1: 2 × 3 = 6 is written in the first box
marks.m2: 11 is written in the second box

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, multiply the primes in each number. The first number is two times three, which is six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The second number is eleven.

beats.on_screen: Step 5, check: 66 ÷ 6 = 11 and 66 ÷ 11 = 6; 6 and 11 share no prime, so HCF = 1

marks.m2: 6 = 2 × 3 and 11 are set side by side with no prime in both

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check. Six goes into sixty six eleven times, and eleven goes into sixty six six times.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six is two times three, and eleven is a prime. They share no prime, so the highest common factor is one.

beats.on_screen: Answer: For example 6 and 11 (also 1 and 66, 2 and 33, 3 and 22)

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Two such numbers are six and eleven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Some other pairs also work for this question. They are one and sixty six, two and thirty three, and three and twenty two.
